payload.throughline: Infer how fast reactions proceed, read the energetic barriers that control rate, separate kinetic path from thermodynamic destination, and predict how reversible systems restore equilibrium.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: infer an order from doubling. This low-stakes check does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: compare experiments that change one concentration at a time, convert the rate factor into an exponent, and verify the assembled rate law against another row.
No prerequisite lesson is declared. All concentration and rate information required for each comparison is supplied.
For rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, m and n are experimentally determined orders. In a controlled pair, the rate factor equals the concentration factor raised to the relevant exponent.
If doubling [A] doubles rate, the reaction is first order in A. If doubling [A] quadruples rate, it is second order in A. If changing [A] leaves rate unchanged, it is zero order in A.
Overall order is the sum of exponents. Rate has concentration-per-time units, so k units are chosen to make the rate-law units balance.
Do not copy balanced-equation coefficients into a rate law unless the prompt establishes an elementary step.
Mental model: controlled experiment pair → concentration factor → rate factor → exponent → assembled law → unit and holdout-row check.
Think aloud: between trials 1 and 2, only [A] doubles and rate rises fourfold. I solve 2^m = 4, so m = 2. I then compare a pair where only [B] changes instead of mixing both effects.

Worked example: trial data show doubling [A] at constant [B] makes rate four times larger, while doubling [B] at constant [A] makes rate twice as large. The rate law is rate = k[A]^2[B], with overall order 3.
Verification: doubling both concentrations predicts an eightfold rate increase: 2^2 × 2 = 8.
Guided practice: use the visible quantity-and-reference frame, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same model with a brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: analyze a fresh chemistry case without answer-bearing help.
Boundary: a large concentration does not imply a large exponent. Order comes from how rate responds to a controlled change, not from one row or a stoichiometric coefficient.
Near exit: apply the taught model independently in a closely aligned case.
Changed exit: preserve the construct while the representation or required operation changes.
Near-function repair: A one-variable comparison isolates one concentration exponent instead of mixing effects. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh near re-entry: recheck the exact function in an unexposed case.
Changed-function repair: Use k units M^(1−n) s^-1 so multiplying by n concentration powers gives M/s. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh changed re-entry: recheck the exact failed function in a new representation.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner.
Recap: isolate one reactant, compare factors, solve the exponent, assemble and verify the law, then balance units for k.
Starting check: predict k from temperature. This low-stakes check does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: distinguish a temperature effect on the rate constant from concentration effects in the rate law, then read activation energy from the Arrhenius form or plot.
No prerequisite lesson is declared. The Arrhenius equation, variable meanings, and plot axes are supplied.
The Arrhenius equation is k = A exp(−Ea/RT). Raising absolute temperature makes −Ea/RT less negative, so k increases when A and Ea are unchanged.
A larger activation energy makes k more temperature-sensitive because the exponential term changes more strongly with 1/T.
Taking logs gives ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T). A plot of ln k versus 1/T is linear with slope −Ea/R and intercept ln A.
Temperature can change k and therefore rate even when concentrations do not change. Use kelvin for Arrhenius relationships.
Mental model: temperature → fraction crossing the activation barrier → rate constant k → reaction rate under the rate law.

Think aloud: temperature rises while concentrations stay fixed. In −Ea/RT, the denominator grows, so the exponent is less negative and k rises. I do not change the experimentally determined reaction orders.

Worked example: two reactions have the same A, but Reaction H has larger Ea than Reaction L. At low temperature H has the smaller k. Raising temperature increases both k values, with the larger proportional change expected for H.
Plot check: H has the more negative slope on ln k versus 1/T because slope magnitude equals Ea/R.
Guided practice: use the visible quantity-and-reference frame, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same model with a brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: analyze a fresh chemistry case without answer-bearing help.
Boundary: a negative Arrhenius-plot slope does not mean k falls as temperature rises; the horizontal axis is 1/T, which decreases when T increases.
Near exit: apply the taught model independently in a closely aligned case.
Changed exit: preserve the construct while the representation or required operation changes.
Near-function repair: Follow the denominator: higher T makes −Ea/RT less negative, so the exponential factor increases. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh near re-entry: recheck the exact function in an unexposed case.
Changed-function repair: Map the linear form directly: y is ln k and x is 1/T. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh changed re-entry: recheck the exact failed function in a new representation.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner.
Recap: use kelvin, follow the exponential sign, separate k from concentration, and read slope as −Ea/R.
Starting check: identify the transition state. This low-stakes check does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: read vertical energy differences from the correct starting level rather than treating every height on the page as the same quantity.
No prerequisite lesson is declared. Each profile supplies reaction direction, energy axis, and intermediate labels.
The left endpoint is the reactant energy and the right endpoint is the product energy for the stated forward direction. A peak represents a transition state.
Forward activation energy is peak energy minus the energy of the species immediately before that step. ΔH is product energy minus reactant energy.
Products below reactants indicate an exothermic forward reaction; products above reactants indicate an endothermic forward reaction.
For a multistep mechanism, compare each peak with its preceding valley. The step with the largest local activation barrier is the rate-determining step in this bounded profile model.
Mental model: endpoint difference gives ΔH; valley-to-next-peak difference gives that step’s activation barrier.
Think aloud: the second peak is highest on the page, but its preceding intermediate is also high. I calculate each local rise from valley to next peak before naming the slow step.
Worked example: reactants are at 20 kJ/mol, the transition state at 70, and products at 5. The forward Ea is 50 kJ/mol, while ΔH is 5−20 = −15 kJ/mol, so the forward reaction is exothermic.
Selection reasoning: the transition-state energy itself is not Ea; Ea is measured from the reactant level.
Guided practice: use the visible quantity-and-reference frame, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same model with a brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: analyze a fresh chemistry case without answer-bearing help.
Boundary: ΔH does not determine reaction speed, and the highest absolute peak is not automatically the largest local barrier in a multistep profile.
Near exit: apply the taught model independently in a closely aligned case.
Changed exit: preserve the construct while the representation or required operation changes.
Near-function repair: Reset the reference at each valley, then measure to the next transition-state peak. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh near re-entry: recheck the exact function in an unexposed case.
Changed-function repair: Keep the references distinct: reactant-to-peak is Ea; reactant-to-product is ΔH. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh changed re-entry: recheck the exact failed function in a new representation.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner.
Recap: label endpoints and peaks, subtract from the correct reference level, separate Ea from ΔH, and compare local barriers step by step.
Starting check: identify a catalyst effect. This low-stakes check does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: separate how fast a pathway is reached from how stable its products are, then decide whether the conditions favor kinetic or thermodynamic control.
No prerequisite lesson is declared. Competing energy profiles and reversibility conditions are supplied.
A catalyst provides an alternate pathway with lower activation energy. It increases forward and reverse rates and shortens the time to equilibrium.
A catalyst does not change reactant or product energies, ΔH, ΔG, or the equilibrium constant K. It does not change the equilibrium composition.
A kinetic product forms faster because its pathway has the lower activation barrier. A thermodynamic product is more stable because it has lower product free energy.
Short times, low temperatures, or irreversible trapping can favor the kinetic product; reversible conditions with enough time can favor the thermodynamic product.
Mental model: barrier height controls speed; endpoint energy controls stability; catalyst changes the path between fixed endpoints.

Think aloud: Product K has the lower transition-state barrier, so it forms faster. Product T lies lower in energy, so it is more stable. I need the time and reversibility conditions before predicting which accumulates.
Worked example: pathways to K and T have barriers of 40 and 70 kJ/mol, while product energies are −10 and −35 kJ/mol relative to reactant. K is the kinetic product; T is the thermodynamic product.
Catalyst check: lowering both barriers can speed formation but does not reverse which product endpoint is lower.
Guided practice: use the visible quantity-and-reference frame, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same model with a brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: analyze a fresh chemistry case without answer-bearing help.
Boundary: “catalyzed” does not mean more product at equilibrium. Faster equilibration and a changed equilibrium position are different claims.
Near exit: apply the taught model independently in a closely aligned case.
Changed exit: preserve the construct while the representation or required operation changes.
Near-function repair: Draw fixed endpoints first; then lower the pathway peak to represent catalysis. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh near re-entry: recheck the exact function in an unexposed case.
Changed-function repair: Use barrier height for kinetic control and product endpoint energy for thermodynamic control. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh changed re-entry: recheck the exact failed function in a new representation.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner.
Recap: read barriers for speed, endpoints for stability, conditions for control, and keep catalyst effects separate from thermodynamics.
Starting check: compare Q with K. This low-stakes check does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: identify what was perturbed, compute or compare Q with K when possible, and predict the reaction direction that restores Q = K.
No prerequisite lesson is declared. Every reaction, phase label, and thermal direction required is supplied.
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the mass-action expression is K = [C]^c[D]^d/([A]^a[B]^b) for the listed solution species. Pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from concentration expressions.

The reaction quotient Q has the same form as K but uses current concentrations. If Q < K, net reaction proceeds forward; if Q > K, net reaction proceeds in reverse; if Q = K, the system is at equilibrium.
Adding a reactant or removing a product lowers Q for a standard product-over-reactant expression and drives the reaction forward. The reverse perturbations drive it backward.
For gases, decreasing volume favors the side with fewer gas moles when the gas-mole counts differ. A catalyst changes approach rate but not K or equilibrium position.
Treat heat as a reaction term for temperature shifts: raising temperature favors the endothermic direction and changes K.
Mental model: perturbation changes Q or K → compare Q with K → choose net direction → stop when Q = K again.
Think aloud: product concentration is suddenly removed, so the product-over-reactant quotient falls below K. The net forward reaction restores product until Q returns to K.
Worked example: for A ⇌ 2B, K = [B]^2/[A]. If current [B]^2/[A] is smaller than K, Q < K and the net reaction proceeds toward B.
Selection reasoning: a catalyst would speed both directions but would not change the Q-versus-K direction or final ratio.
Guided practice: use the visible quantity-and-reference frame, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same model with a brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: analyze a fresh chemistry case without answer-bearing help.
Boundary: equilibrium is dynamic, not a state of zero reactions. Equal forward and reverse rates can maintain constant concentrations while molecules continue reacting.
Near exit: apply the taught model independently in a closely aligned case.
Changed exit: preserve the construct while the representation or required operation changes.
Near-function repair: Anchor the comparison: Q below K needs more products; Q above K needs more reactants. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh near re-entry: recheck the exact function in an unexposed case.
Changed-function repair: A catalyst changes how quickly Q reaches K, not the value of K or the final composition. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh changed re-entry: recheck the exact failed function in a new representation.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner.
Recap: write the expression, form Q from current conditions, compare with K, predict the restoring direction, and keep catalysts separate from shifts.
